source.title: What 30,000 Hours of Ego-centric Video Does Not Teach
source.authors: Jia-Hua Dong; Anurag Bagchi; Yash Jangir; Muhammad Zubair Irshad; Sergey Zakharov; Martial Hebert; Homanga Bharadhwaj; Yu-Xiong Wang; V. Guizilini; P. Tokmakov

record.file_problem: none; the complete paper text and appendices are present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper measures scaling behavior in video world models using agent/object SCS, rather than held-out language-model cross-entropy. This is a conceptual test of scaling-form behavior in another modality, not a reproduction of the language-model measurements.
record.gate_note: The study tests data and model scaling in ego-centric video world models, not language-model loss or compute-optimal parameter/token allocation. It cites scaling-law analyses when fitting saturating curves, but reports no results on language models. Raw point values in Figure 4 and Figure 5 are not transcribed where the text gives only curve summaries.
record.test_reason: The study trains video diffusion world models (Cosmos 3 Edge 4B, Nano 16B, Super 64B) on a nested 300 to 30k hour ego-centric video ladder. It fits a saturating power law S∞ − cD^−α to fidelity (SCS) versus data. This is a new setting (video world models) with a result on V5. The measure is a regional structural-fidelity score, not held-out loss. The study's purpose is interaction fidelity, not scaling laws, so T3 fits better than T2. It gives no language-model loss results, so V1–V4, V6 and V7 are not tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors conclude that scaling ego-centric data improves both agent and object fidelity, but agent fidelity saturates near its limit (reachable far more cheaply via skeleton conditioning), while object fidelity converges far lower. A 4× model increase barely helps, and closing the gap would take about 6 further quadruplings. They add that their supervision scheme raises the object ceiling only partially, so progress depends on how models are trained, not only on how much data they see.
record.recipe_differences: The study scales video world models and measures regional SCS, rather than language-model held-out cross-entropy, parameter/token/compute laws, or compute-optimal allocations. It fits saturating curves to SCS.
record.method_sensitivity: The apparent object-scaling curve depends on skeleton conditioning: the baseline object curve has no comparable deceleration within the tested range, while the skeleton-conditioned curve decelerates and has a fitted asymptote. Data exposure and optimizer updates are coupled in the ladder.

fits_no_version.finding: Skeleton conditioning reaches baseline agent fidelity with about 50× less data but converges to nearly the same asymptote. Object-centric noise scheduling raises the object ceiling without changing the rate at which it is approached.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Conditioning and supervision design shift the data-efficiency offset or the asymptote of a saturating scaling curve independently of its exponent.

record.code_released: The authors say they will publicly release the code, checkpoints, and evaluation benchmark; no code URL is stated.
record.problems: The data ladder spans two orders of magnitude and couples data exposure with optimization budget. The reported scaling results use SCS rather than loss, and the authors note that the fitted ceilings depend on the fitted regime continuing beyond 30k hours. The evaluation set is limited in scale and both data sets use a single collection protocol.
record.rows_left_out: No additional result rows omitted. Figure-only point values from Figures 4 and 5 are not separately transcribed; the rows record the curve summaries and values stated in the text.

untested.parts: Held-out loss scaling (only SCS/LPIPS fidelity metrics are used); image models; repeated data; fine-tuning and transfer as power-law relations; compute scaling separated from data (they are coupled); parameter scaling beyond a single 4× step.
Not tested: no language-model pretraining loss.
Not tested: no check that small-run fits predict larger runs.
Not tested: no fixed-compute allocation sweep.
Not tested: no depth/width variation at fixed parameters.
Not tested: the humanoid transfer results are not related to scale or loss.
Not tested: no comparison of fitting choices. The authors only note that coupling data with steps makes the fitted ceilings optimistic.

missing.what: Nano baseline object SCS gain of +0.14 across the ladder (versus Edge +0.10); currently misattributed in R3.
LPIPS versus training exposure also saturates across the data ladder: a perceptual-quality scaling curve.

Object SCS with dynamic-region supervision across the ladder: 0.546 vs 0.527 at 30k hours, with a higher fitted asymptote. This is the study's own method, so it is a method comparison rather than a scaling row.

record.verdict_notes: The fitted curves use the Kaplan/Hoffmann-style form with an irreducible term, but on a fidelity metric, over only 5 points spanning two orders of magnitude. The checkpoints come from a single constant-learning-rate run, so data and compute are coupled; the authors say this makes the fitted ceilings optimistic. No fit uncertainty or goodness of fit is reported. Edge differs in design and pretraining, so the authors do not treat it as a capacity trend.

versions.untested_parts: No language-model held-out pretraining loss, parameter/token/compute scaling, or bottleneck conditions are measured.
The paper fits saturating curves and reports asymptotes, but does not test whether fits on small runs predict substantially larger runs.
No fixed-compute allocation sweep or loss-minimising parameter/token split is tested.
The paper does not isolate depth, width, or other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
Tests ego-centric video world models using SCS, not held-out loss; does not test image models, repeated data, fine-tuning, or transfer as instances of a power-law loss relation.
Downstream humanoid results are reported, but the study does not test whether downstream performance is predictable from scale or pretraining loss.
The study notes that data exposure and optimization budget are coupled, but does not compare fitting choices or establish disagreement in exponents or compute-optimal splits.

rows.subject: Nano
rows.stage_stated: video diffusion world model trained on ego-centric human video
rows.operation_detail: Measured agent SCS across the nested training-data ladder; text reports gains over portions of the ladder and a fitted saturating-curve asymptote.
rows.value: Gain of 0.12 SCS between 300 and 3k hours and 0.06 between 3k and 30k; fitted asymptote 0.811.
rows.note: The paper describes agent fidelity as visibly saturating and fits S∞ − cD−α. Data exposure and optimization compute increase together.
rows.check: OK. Note the fit is to SCS, a fidelity metric, not loss. No goodness of fit is reported, and data exposure is coupled with optimizer steps under a constant learning rate.

source_check.locator_found: Section 4, Figure 4 discussion: baseline agent gains and fitted asymptote 0.811.

rows.subject: Nano
rows.stage_stated: video diffusion world model trained on ego-centric human video
rows.operation_detail: Measured agent SCS across the nested training-data ladder with skeleton conditioning.
rows.baseline: Baseline conditioning reaches the same agent fidelity at roughly 15k hours.
rows.value: At 300 hours, reaches the baseline's roughly 15k-hour agent fidelity; gains 0.06 over the remaining two orders of magnitude; the two designs converge to 0.811 and 0.800, respectively.
rows.note: The text says skeleton conditioning changes when the agent limit is reached, not what that limit is.
rows.check: OK. Both conditioning designs converge to similar fitted asymptotes (0.811 vs 0.800); the curve is shifted roughly 50× in data.

source_check.locator_found: Section 4, conditioning discussion: 300 versus roughly 15k hours; gain 0.06; skeleton-conditioned asymptote 0.800.

rows.subject: Nano
rows.stage_stated: video diffusion world model trained on ego-centric human video
rows.operation_detail: Measured manipulated-object SCS across the nested training-data ladder.
rows.baseline: At 300 hours, the skeleton-conditioned variant's object fidelity matches the baseline's fidelity at 3k hours.
rows.value: Object fidelity improves by 0.09 across two orders of magnitude; the paper reports no comparable deceleration and says the asymptote is undetermined within the tested range.
rows.note: The reported curve does not establish an asymptote in this condition; point values are shown in the figure.
rows.check: Value is wrong. The 0.09 gain over two orders of magnitude is the skeleton-conditioned figure, which is R4. The text gives the Nano baseline object gain as +0.14 (versus +0.10 for Edge). The baseline field is also wrong: it describes the skeleton variant, not a baseline. The paper says the baseline object curve shows no deceleration and does not constrain an asymptote, so the fit of the power-law form cannot be judged for this condition.

source_check.correct: Nano baseline object SCS improves by 0.14 across the data ladder; 0.09 belongs to skeleton-conditioned Nano. The baseline object asymptote remains undetermined. Skeleton-conditioned Nano at 300 hours reaches baseline object fidelity at 3k hours.
source_check.locator_found: Section 4, opening paragraph and Figure 4 discussion of baseline and skeleton-conditioned object scaling.
source_check.problem: The 0.09 gain is assigned to the wrong conditioning.

rows.subject: Nano
rows.stage_stated: video diffusion world model trained on ego-centric human video
rows.operation_detail: Measured manipulated-object SCS across the nested training-data ladder with skeleton conditioning; fitted a saturating curve.
rows.value: Improves by 0.09 across two orders of magnitude; gains 0.056 from 300 to 3k hours and 0.035 from 3k to 30k; fitted asymptote 0.565, with 93% of that level reached at 30k hours.
rows.note: This is an asymptotic fit to SCS, not a fit to language-model cross-entropy.
rows.check: OK. Fitted asymptote 0.565, with 93% of it reached at 30k hours.

source_check.locator_found: Section 4, skeleton-conditioned object scaling: gains 0.09 overall, 0.056 and 0.035 by interval; asymptote 0.565; 93% reached.

rows.subject: Edge
rows.stage_stated: video diffusion world model; denoising transformer trained from scratch
rows.operation_detail: Measured object fidelity across the data ladder.
rows.value: Improvement of 0.10 across the data range.
rows.note: The paper reports this as the Edge object-fidelity gain when comparing Edge with Nano; it does not give an Edge-specific fitted asymptote in the text.
rows.check: The text gives only the +0.10 gain over the ladder, with no fit and no curve shape. Improvement with data is shown, but the power-law form cannot be read.

source_check.locator_found: Section 4, opening paragraph: Nano versus Edge baseline object improvements of 0.14 versus 0.10.

rows.subject: Super
rows.stage_stated: video diffusion world model; adapted from a pretrained Qwen3-VL variant
rows.operation_detail: Compared model capacity with the Nano variant at the larger model size.
rows.value: Raising model size by a factor of 4 raises the object ceiling by 0.034 SCS points.
rows.note: The paper estimates that closing the remaining 0.205 to the agent ceiling would require roughly 6 further quadruplings, assuming the gain per quadrupling does not diminish.
rows.check: This is a single two-point model-size comparison (Nano vs Super, 4×), so no power law in parameters can be fit. It gives a +0.034 gain in the fitted object ceiling.

source_check.correct: Super raises the fitted object ceiling by 0.034 SCS relative to Nano with skeleton conditioning. V5 state: cannot_determine; the two-size comparison does not establish a power-law form in parameter count.
source_check.locator_found: Section 3.1, Nano/Super capacity comparison; Section 4, final paragraph spanning pages 7–8.
source_check.problem: A small ceiling increase across two model sizes does not establish partial occurrence of V5's power-law form.

rows.subject: Super
rows.stage_stated: video diffusion world model; adapted from a pretrained Qwen3-VL variant
rows.operation_detail: Compared agent fidelity with the Nano variant at the larger model size.
rows.value: Virtually no effect on agent fidelity.
rows.note: Super is reported with skeleton conditioning only.
rows.check: No value is given: the text says only 'virtually no effect' on agent SCS from a 4× model increase. This is a single two-point comparison.

source_check.correct: The fourfold Nano-to-Super increase has virtually no effect on agent fidelity. V5 state: cannot_determine; this two-size comparison does not determine whether parameter scaling follows a power law.
source_check.locator_found: Section 3.1, Super evaluated only with skeleton conditioning; Section 4, final paragraph.
source_check.problem: Negligible improvement is reported, but it does not establish absence of V5's power-law form.

relationships.condition: Nano data scaling (300–30k h) of agent SCS with both conditionings, and object SCS with skeleton conditioning, in ego-centric video world models
relationships.reason: Fidelity rises with data and decelerates. Saturating power-law fits give identifiable asymptotes: 0.811/0.800 for the agent and 0.565 for objects (R1, R2, R4).
relationships.display_finding: Fidelity increased with diminishing gains, with saturating power-law asymptotes of 0.811 and 0.800 for agents and 0.565 for objects.

relationships.condition: Model-size scaling (Nano→Super, 4×) and baseline-conditioned object fidelity
relationships.reason: A 4× model increase barely moves agent SCS and adds only 0.034 to the object ceiling (R6, R7). The baseline object curves cannot constrain the form or asymptote within range (R3, R5). The measure is SCS, not loss, and data is coupled with optimizer steps.
relationships.display_finding: A fourfold size increase barely changed agent SCS and raised the object ceiling by 0.034, while baseline object curves left the scaling form and asymptote unconstrained.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.condition: Model-size scaling (Nano→Super, 4×) and baseline-conditioned object fidelity
source_check.reason: R3 and R5 leave the baseline object functional form undetermined; R6 and R7 compare only two model sizes. Neither weak gains nor an unidentified asymptote demonstrates failure of a power-law form. These are unresolved tests, not established scope limits.
